reading.rtitle: Options note -- the south, before the November board
paras: Diane, you asked for options, not a decision, so here are two. Coverage in the south is behind plan, and the reason is clear: the first visit to a new workshop is expensive, and the south has more new workshops than any other region. We could fix this in two different ways, and neither of them is free.

Option one. We could move one field team from the north to the south for the first quarter. It costs nothing extra, because the team already exists, and coverage in the south might go up by three or four points before March. The downside is the north. It is ahead of plan today, and it might fall behind if we take the team away for three months.

Option two. We could hire a second field team for the south only. It is the more expensive alternative, and the budget is tight, but the north stays as it is and the upside is bigger in the long run. The risk is time: hiring might take two months, so we would not see results before April. I would suggest option one as a pilot for one quarter, and we could consider option two in the budget for next year. It is a compromise, but I think it is feasible. Could we talk about it on Thursday?

listenings.text: When a director comes into my office and says we must do this, my first reaction is to look for the problem with it. I cannot help it. Must is a closed door, and people want to open closed doors. When the same director says we could do this, and here is what it might cost us, my reaction is completely different. I start thinking about how to make it work, because the idea is still open and I am part of it. So my advice to anyone with a proposal is simple. Bring two options, not one. Say what each one could do and what might go wrong. Then say which one you would suggest, and why. You will get more yes answers with could and might than you ever got with must, and the strange thing is that people will think you are more confident, not less.

There is a difference between could and might that a lot of people miss, even native speakers. Could is about what is possible. It opens a door. We could move a team, we could hire, we could wait. Might is about what is uncertain. It warns you about the other side of the door. Coverage might go up. The north might fall behind. Hiring might take two months. In a good proposal you need both. Could gives the room options, and might shows the room that you have already thought about the risk. And one more thing about the end of a proposal. Do not finish with a statement. Finish with a question, like could we talk about it on Thursday, or might this work for your team. A question at the end gives the decision back to the room, and a room that decides is a room that supports you.
